title: Honoring guests
tomorrow: Dadi insists on carrying the heavy pot herself. do you let her?

segments.voice: Yesterday, reconnect: the keeper of the tie is the one who joins it again. Today the door opens the other way. Someone's coming in.

Before guests arrive, a house has a smell. Onions going soft. Cardamom cracked for coffee. Something in the oven a little longer than planned. So what gets made first? In the Qur'an, Abraham answers without a speech. Strangers come to his door and say peace. He says peace back, and then, before anyone has explained who they are, he slips away to his household and comes back with a fatted calf.
screen: `ONIONS, CARDAMOM, THE OVEN.` → `STRANGERS SAY PEACE.` → `A CALF, BEFORE NAMES.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an asks it as a question, in Pickthall's words: "Hath the story of Abraham's honoured guests reached thee?" He doesn't ask for names first. He doesn't check what they're owed. He brings the food and sets it before them himself, and says: "Will ye not eat?" The honor is in the hurry and the setting-down. The Prophet ﷺ made it part of faith. In Sahih al-Bukhari: whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest. Another report gives it a shape: a day and a night of your best, and hospitality for up to three days. Notice how much of it is the senses. A guest is honored through the nose, the mouth and the hands before much is said: coffee smelled at the door, a plate set down, a seat pulled out. And here's something a Christian or Jewish neighbor would recognize. Abraham's visitors appear in the book of Genesis too, where he runs to meet strangers at his tent and hurries to bring bread and a calf. One open tent, remembered in more than one scripture. One to tell a friend tonight: in the Qur'an, Abraham feeds his guests before he knows who they are.
screen: `ABRAHAM'S HONORED GUESTS.` · `WILL YE NOT EAT?` · `HONOR YOUR GUEST.` · `AN OPEN TENT IN GENESIS TOO.` · then, large: `HONOR GUESTS.`

segments.voice: If there's something to drink or eat near you, coffee, tea, water, a date, take one slow sip or bite as if you were the guest. Notice the warmth or the cool, the taste, and what it would mean if someone had made it for you before asking your name. Then picture setting the same cup down in front of someone else.
screen: `ONE SLOW SIP, AS THE GUEST.` · `MADE BEFORE YOUR NAME.` · `THEN, SET IT DOWN FOR SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: Honoring guests: welcoming and feeding whoever comes to the door, before the questions. Abraham brought the calf first.
Your line: honor guests, and let the coffee come before the questions. Eight of ten.

sources.ref: Qur'an 51:25–27 (they said peace; he went to his household, brought a fatted calf and set it before them)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6018–6019 (whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest; the guest's due is a day and a night; hospitality is three days)
Genesis 18:1–8 (Abraham runs to meet three men at his tent and brings bread and a calf)

notes: Confirm the exact Pickthall wording of 51:24 ('Hath the story of Abraham's honoured guests reached thee (O Muhammad)?'; the parenthesis is left out) and 51:27 ('Will ye not eat?').
Bukhari 6018-6019: confirm numbering and paraphrase ('a day and a night of your best, and hospitality for up to three days').

Genesis 18:1-8 paraphrased; 'appear in Genesis too' is a light unity note (a neighbor's own scripture), not ranking. Muslim and Jewish/Christian tellings differ in detail (the Qur'an doesn't count the guests); the voice gives no count.
The hook's 'before anyone has explained who they are': in 51:25 they say peace and he calls them 'folk unknown'; confirm.
